title: Arrays of objects and custom sorting
overview: Module 7 stores many objects in an array and sorts them with your own rules. You write comparator functions, handle ties with a second key, find min/max objects, and practise small problems that mix strings, functions and counting.

concepts.explain: `Student a[n];` gives n objects; reach fields with `a[i].field`.
A function `bool cmp(T l, T r)` that says whether `l` should come before `r`.
concepts.snippet: bool cmp(Student l, Student r) { return l.marks > r.marks; }

concepts.explain: Compare the main key; when equal, compare the second key.
concepts.snippet: return l.marks == r.marks ? l.roll < r.roll : l.marks > r.marks;

concepts.explain: Keep a whole object as the best so far and replace it when a better one appears.
Adding or subtracting 1 flips even/odd, so counting parities solves Even Hate Odd.

files.title: Array of objects
files.what: Stores many students in `Student a[n]` and fills each element's fields in a loop - first with one-word names, then with full names read by `getline`.
steps: `Student a[n];` makes n objects.
`cin >> a[i].name >> a[i].roll >> a[i].marks;` fills each one.
For the second array, `cin.ignore()` then `getline(cin, a2[i].name)` reads names with spaces.
Print both arrays.
files.input:
2
Rahim 1 80
Karim 2 75
2
Sakib Al Hasan
75 88
Tamim Iqbal
29 91
files.input_note: n and n lines `name roll marks`; then n2 and, for each student, a name line and a `roll marks` line.
files.output_note: First part: `Rahim 1 80`, `Karim 2 75`. Second part: `Sakib Al Hasan 7588` - roll and marks are glued because the print has no space between them.
files.watch_out: The second print is missing a space: write `<< " " << a2[i].marks`.

check.q: Why does `cin.ignore()` sit inside the loop before `getline`?
check.a: Each `cin >> marks` leaves a newline, which must be skipped before the next name line.

files.title: Min and max object by marks
files.what: Finds the student with the lowest and the highest marks by keeping a whole `Student` as the best so far.
steps: Start `min_obj.marks = INT_MAX`; replace `min_obj` with any student who has fewer marks.
Start `max_obj.marks = INT_MIN`; replace it with anyone who has more.
Print both objects.
files.input_note: n, then n lines `name roll marks`.
files.output_note: It does not compile, so there is no output. After the fix it would print `Rina 3 60` (min) and `Joy 2 95` (max).
files.watch_out: `min(min_marks, a[i].name)` compares an `int` with a `string` and fails to compile. It should be `a[i].marks` (or delete that unused loop).

check.a: So the first student always has fewer marks and replaces it.

files.title: Sorting objects with a comparator
files.what: `sort` does not know how to order students, so you pass a comparator function: `dsc` for highest marks first, `asc` for lowest first.
steps: `bool dsc(Student l, Student r)` returns true when `l` should come before `r` (`l.marks > r.marks`).
`sort(a, a+n, dsc)` sorts by marks, highest first.
`sort(a, a+n, asc)` sorts lowest first.
Print after each sort.
files.input:
6
Rakib 3 76
Sakib 2 80
Maruf 1 99
Nakib 4 60
Nakib 5 50
Ropon 6 45
files.input_note: n, then n lines `name roll marks`.
files.output_note: First block from Maruf 99 down to Ropon 45; second block is the reverse, from Ropon 45 up to Maruf 99.

check.a: `true` if the first argument should come before the second, otherwise `false`.

files.title: Tie-breaking comparators (three styles)
files.what: Writes the same rule - marks descending, then roll ascending - as if/else (`dsc`), with `==` first (`dsc2`) and as a one-line ternary (`dsc3`).
steps: If marks differ, the bigger mark comes first.
If marks are equal, the smaller roll comes first.
`dsc3` packs it into `(l.marks == r.marks) ? l.roll < r.roll : l.marks > r.marks`.
`main` reads and prints the students.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) if sorted
files.input_note: n, then n lines `name roll marks`.
files.output_note: It does not compile, so there is no output. With the fix and a `sort` call you would get `Joy 12 99`, `Rina 7 90`, `Sakib 5 86`, `Asif 29 86`.
files.watch_out: A second function also named `dsc` (the ascending version) causes "redefinition of dsc". Rename it (for example `asc`). `main` also never calls `sort`; add `sort(a, a + n, dsc);` before printing.

check.q: Using `dsc3`, which comes first: (marks 86, roll 29) or (marks 86, roll 5)?
check.a: Roll 5, because on equal marks the smaller roll comes first.

files.title: Practice: sort students by marks, then roll
files.what: Sorts students by marks (high to low) and breaks ties by roll (low to high).
steps: Read `n` students.
`dsc`: if marks are equal return `l.roll < r.roll`, else `l.marks > r.marks`.
`sort(a, a+n, dsc)` and print.
files.input_note: n, then n lines `name roll marks`.
files.output_note: `Joy 12 99`, `Asif 29 95`, then the three students with 86 in roll order 39, 55, 57.
files.watch_out: The two comment lines with a Codeium tag are editor leftovers and can be deleted.

check.q: Why is the tie rule needed even though `sort` would still give a sorted result without it?
check.a: Without it, students with equal marks could appear in any order; the task asks for roll order.

files.title: Practice: count a word in a sentence
files.what: Reads the word first, then the sentence, and counts exact matches using `stringstream`.
steps: `cin >> name` reads the word; `cin.ignore()` drops the newline.
`getline(cin, words)` reads the sentence.
`while (ss3 >> word)` compares each word with `name`.
files.input:
john
Sanju john samson John takla john baby
files.input_note: Line 1: the word to find. Line 2: the sentence.
files.output_note: Prints `2`: `john` appears twice; `John` with a capital J does not count.
files.watch_out: The comment at the top says the sentence comes first, but the code reads the word first. Keep the input order the code expects.

check.a: Yes, `==` on strings compares exact characters.

files.title: N Times
files.what: A function builds a string with the character repeated n times, separated by spaces.
steps: `generateString(n, c)` appends `c`, and a space except after the last one.
`main` stores each result in `outputs` and prints them after all input.
files.output_note: `n`, `O O O O O`, `z z z`.

check.q: Why check `i != n-1` before adding a space?
check.a: To avoid a trailing space after the last character.

files.title: Even Hate Odd

problem.name: Codeforces group - G. Even Hate Odd

files.what: Each +1 or -1 turns one number from even to odd or back. So the answer is how far the even count is from n/2; odd n is impossible.
steps: If `n` is odd, read and ignore the numbers and answer -1.
Count the even numbers.
The answer is `abs(even_count - n/2)`.
Print all answers at the end.
files.input_note: t; for each test n and the array.
files.output_note: `1 2 3 4` is already balanced (0), `1 1 1 1` needs 2 changes, and n = 3 is impossible (-1).
files.watch_out: `int a[100001]` inside the loop takes about 400 KB of stack; it works, but declaring it outside `main` is safer.

check.q: Why is one operation enough to fix one element?
check.a: Adding or subtracting 1 always flips a number's parity.

recap: Pass a comparator as the third argument to `sort` for objects.
A comparator returns true when the first item should come first.
Break ties with a second key to get a fixed order.
Two functions can't share the same name and parameters.
Check that you compare the right field (`marks`, not `name`).

check_yourself.q: Write a comparator that sorts students by roll ascending.
check_yourself.a: `bool cmp(Student l, Student r) { return l.roll < r.roll; }`

check_yourself.q: What happens if your comparator returns true for equal elements (uses `>=`)?
check_yourself.a: It breaks the rules `sort` needs and can cause wrong results or crashes; use strict `>` or `<`.

check_yourself.q: How do you read a name with spaces into `a[i].name` after reading numbers?
